rewritten_text:
‘Well, Huck, that's how everybody lives.’

‘That don't matter, Tom. I ain't everybody, and I can't bear it. Being hemmed in that way is terrible. And food's too easy to get—I don't care a thing about eating when it's like that. I have to ask before I go fishing, and ask before I go swimming—darned if I don't have to ask before I do anything at all. And I had to speak so proper it took all the pleasure out of talking. Every day I had to sneak into the attic and cuss a while, just to get the taste back in my mouth. I'd have died otherwise, Tom. The widow wouldn't let me smoke or holler, or yawn, or stretch, or scratch myself with people around—’ Then, with a fresh burst of wounded irritation, he added, ‘And blame her, she was always praying! I never knew a woman like her. I had to clear out, Tom. There wasn't anything else to do. Besides, school's about to start, and she'd have made me go. Well, I wouldn't put up with that, Tom. Listen, being rich ain't nearly what folks say. It's nothing but fretting and sweating and wishing you were dead. These clothes are good enough for me, and so's this barrel, and I ain't ever giving them up again. Tom, none of this trouble would have come if it weren't for that money. You take my share along with yours and give me a dime now and then—not often, because I don't care a darn about anything unless it's fairly hard to get. And go ask the widow to let me off.’

‘Oh, Huck, you know I couldn't. It wouldn't be right. Besides, stick at it a little longer and you'll get to liking it.’

‘Liking it! Sure, the way I'd get to liking a hot stove by sitting on it long enough. No, Tom, I won't be rich, and I won't stay in those blasted houses that choke a fellow. Give me the woods and the river and big barrels; I'm sticking with them. Confound it! Just when we'd got guns and a cave and everything ready to start robbing, this darned nonsense had to turn up and ruin the whole thing!’

Tom recognized his chance.

‘Look here, Huck, being rich won't stop me from becoming a robber.’

‘It won't? Oh, splendid! Do you really mean it, Tom, honest and true?’

‘As surely as I'm sitting here. But you know, Huck, we can't take you into the gang unless you're respectable.’

Huck's happiness died away.

‘You can't take me in, Tom?’

‘They ought to concern you, Dorian. Every gentleman cares about his reputation. You cannot wish to be spoken of as vile and debased. Naturally, you possess wealth and standing and all the rest, but those are not the whole of life. Understand me: I put no faith in these rumours. Or at least, I cannot credit them with you before my eyes. A man's sins inscribe themselves upon his face; they will not stay hidden. We hear people speak of secret vices, but such things do not exist. If some miserable fellow has a vice, it appears in the lines about his lips, in his lowered eyelids, even in the form of his hands. Last year someone—you know him, though I shall withhold his name—asked me to paint his portrait. I had neither met him nor heard anything of him then, although I have learned plenty since. The sum he offered was extravagant. I turned him away. Something about the shape of his fingers repelled me. I know today that my instinct about him was entirely justified. He leads a dreadful life. Yet you, Dorian, with that clear, innocent, radiant face and your wonderful, untroubled youth—I cannot believe a word spoken against you. Still, I scarcely see you nowadays; you no longer visit the studio. And when you are absent and I hear the horrible stories being whispered about you, I have no idea how to answer. Why, Dorian, does someone like the Duke of Berwick walk out of a club room as soon as you come in? Why do so many London gentlemen refuse either to visit you or to receive you in their homes? Lord Staveley was once your friend. I encountered him at dinner last week, and your name arose when we were discussing the miniatures you lent to the Dudley exhibition. Staveley's lip curled. He said your artistic taste might be exquisite, but you were a man no innocent girl ought to meet and no virtuous woman ought to share a room with. I told him I was your friend and demanded to know his meaning. He explained. In front of everyone, without reserve, he explained. It was appalling! Why does your friendship bring such ruin to young men? Think of that unfortunate boy in the Guards who took his own life. You were an intimate friend of his. Then there was Sir Henry Ashton, forced to quit England with his reputation disgraced.’

‘I will move on now to the more deeply moving part of my story. I will describe the events that left me with the feelings that changed me from what I once was into what I am now.

‘Spring progressed quickly. The weather grew fine, and the skies cleared. I was astonished to see ground that had been bleak and empty burst into beautiful flowers and greenery. Countless delightful scents and lovely sights pleased and refreshed my senses.

‘On one of the days when the cottagers took their regular break from work, the old man played his guitar while his children listened. I noticed an indescribable sadness in Felix's face. He kept sighing, and once his father stopped playing. From the old man's manner, I guessed that he was asking why his son was unhappy. Felix answered cheerfully. His father was beginning to play again when someone knocked at the door.

‘A lady had arrived on horseback, accompanied by a countryman who acted as her guide. She wore a dark outfit and a thick black veil. Agatha asked her something, but the stranger answered only by saying Felix's name in a sweet voice. Her voice was musical, though unlike those of either of my friends. Hearing his name, Felix hurried toward her. When she saw him, she raised her veil, revealing a face whose beauty and expression seemed angelic. Her shining, raven-black hair was arranged in intricate braids. Her dark eyes were gentle despite their liveliness; her features were evenly proportioned, and her complexion was wonderfully fair, with a delicate pink in both cheeks.

‘Felix seemed overwhelmed with happiness at the sight of her. Every trace of sadness left his face, instantly replaced by a joy so ecstatic that I would scarcely have believed him capable of showing it. His eyes shone, and his cheeks flushed with pleasure. At that moment I thought him as beautiful as the stranger. She seemed to be feeling something different. Wiping a few tears from her lovely eyes, she extended her hand. Felix kissed it passionately and called her, as far as I could make out, his sweet Arabian. She did not seem to understand, but she smiled. He helped her off the horse, dismissed her guide, and brought her into the cottage. He and his father spoke for a while. Then the young woman knelt at the old man's feet and tried to kiss his hand, but he helped her up and embraced her affectionately.

‘I soon realized that although the stranger spoke clearly formed words and seemed to have a language of her own, the people in the cottage could not understand her, and she could not understand them.’
